# On the Strange Beauty of Small Decisions

I've been thinking lately about the moments that reshape us—not the dramatic ones that make headlines in our own minds, but the quiet decisions that slip past almost unnoticed. The choice to take a different route home. To call someone back instead of deleting the message. To try the coffee shop you've walked past a hundred times. These are the hinges upon which lives turn, I think, though we rarely acknowledge it while they're happening.

There's something almost comforting about this idea, actually. It means we're not entirely subject to fate or grand destiny. We're constantly, minutely steering ourselves through existence with these small acts of intention. And it means that the life you're living right now isn't the only possible life—it's just the one that resulted from an infinite series of tiny choices, many of which you've probably already forgotten.

I wonder sometimes what alternate versions of myself exist in the probability space of the multiverse, if such a thing exists. There's a me who took the job in Portland. A me who married someone different, or didn't marry at all. A me who learned the guitar seriously instead of putting it down after two weeks of aching fingers. These shadow selves are neither better nor worse—they're just different expressions of the same central consciousness, shaped by different coordinates on the map of possibility.

What strikes me most is that none of these theoretical versions would feel like they were living the consolation-prize version of their life. Each one would have their own arc, their own meaning, their own sense of rightness or wrongness about the path they'd taken. The version of me in Portland probably has moments of wondering what would have happened if I'd stayed here instead. We're all convinced, I think, that we made the choice we made, and that it mattered somehow, even when we can barely remember making it.

This is why nostalgia is so bittersweet. It's not just missing the past—it's mourning the fact that you can never fully understand it. You can remember what happened, but you can't fully recapture what it *felt* like to not know what would happen next. That young person who was deciding something—deciding to go to that party, deciding to study that subject, deciding to trust someone—they lived in a moment of genuine uncertainty. But when you look back, you can only see the person who made the choice and its aftermath. The actual moment of decision is opaque to you now. You've crossed through it and can't go back to the threshold.

I think this is why we tell stories so much. We're trying to reconstruct the feeling of meaningful uncertainty, even though we're narrating from a point where the outcome is already known. The best stories manage to create that sense of not-knowing even though we're reading forward through time and could look ahead if we wanted. There's an art to making the destination feel uncertain even after you've arrived.

Lately I've been paying more attention to the way my thoughts move. Not the content of thoughts so much as the texture of thinking itself. How sometimes your mind is racing ahead of you, jumping ten steps into the future, while your body is still inhabiting the present moment. How sometimes you'll suddenly realize you've been thinking the same thought for five minutes on repeat without actually progressing it. How thoughts seem to arise in you almost unbidden—you don't decide to think them so much as discover you're already thinking them.

This makes the illusion of control feel paper-thin sometimes. How much of what we "decide" is actually just us noticing what we've already decided? When someone asks what you want for dinner and you hear yourself say "Thai food," did you decide that, or did the thought arrive fully formed and you just reported it? The philosophical question feels important somehow, even though I have no idea how to answer it.

I've also become fascinated by the concept of "found time"—those moments when you discover that something takes less effort or time than you'd anticipated, and suddenly you have this unexpected pocket of freedom. You sit down expecting to spend an hour on some task, and twenty minutes later you're done. There's this strange little gift of unscheduled time. It's never much, but there's something about it that feels more valuable than scheduled leisure time, even though they're the same minutes. Maybe it's the surprise of it. Maybe it's that it's genuinely free rather than being time you'd already allocated.

I think we don't talk enough about pleasure. Not sexual pleasure, though that too, but ordinary pleasure. The pleasure of good light through a window. The pleasure of finishing a piece of writing you're satisfied with. The pleasure of a conversation where you feel truly understood. We have this cultural tendency to treat pleasure as somehow frivolous—as though serious, meaningful people shouldn't waste time on it. But I think pleasure is actually incredibly important information. It's what tells you what's worth doing.

The things that bring you genuine pleasure are usually pointing at something true about who you are and what matters to you. If you take pleasure in helping people, you're getting information about your values. If you take pleasure in learning, in creating, in moving your body, in understanding how things work—these aren't distractions from meaning, they're where meaning lives.

So much of my anxiety, I think, comes from not listening to this information. From trying to do things that look meaningful from the outside rather than things that actually produce that internal sense of rightness. And the weird thing is that the guilt about not doing something productive usually prevents me from enjoying whatever it is I *am* doing. So you lose twice—once because you're not doing the thing that would feel meaningful, and again because you're not present for what you are doing.

I don't have any grand conclusions here. Just observations about how we move through time, how we decide, how we try to make meaning from contingency. How we're all improvising constantly, acting as though our choices matter because in the moment before we make them, they actually do. And then we move forward into the consequences, and those consequences become who we are, until we make the next small decision that will ripple outward in ways we'll never fully understand.

It's strange being alive. I'm grateful for it, most days.
